## A. Prepare GDP per capita data

This opening block prepares the GDP per capita data for analysis.

```r
gdppc <- global_economy |>
  mutate(GDP_per_capita = GDP / Population) |>
  select(Year, Country, GDP, Population, GDP_per_capita)

gdppc
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Calculates GDP per capita by dividing GDP by Population.
- Selects relevant columns to create a clean tsibble.
- Displays the resulting data structure.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- The data includes multiple countries over time.
- GDP per capita is a derived variable for per-person economic output.
:::

## B. Visualize GDP per capita for Sweden

This section visualizes the data for a specific country.

```r
gdppc |>
  filter(Country == "Sweden") |>
  autoplot(GDP_per_capita) +
  labs(title = "GDP per capita for Sweden", y = "$US")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Filters the data to Sweden only.
- Plots the GDP per capita over time with appropriate labels.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Look for trends, cycles, or changes in the series.
- Consider the scale and units of the y-axis.
:::

## C. Fit naive and drift models

This block fits simple forecasting models to the data.

```r
fit <- gdppc |>
  model(naive = NAIVE(GDP_per_capita),
        drift_method = RW(GDP_per_capita ~ drift())
        )

fit
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Fits a naive model (last value repeated) and a random walk with drift.
- Creates a model table (mable) for all countries.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- The models are fitted to each country separately.
- Compare the model specifications.
:::

## D. Generate forecasts

This section produces forecasts from the fitted models.

```r
fc <- fit |> forecast(h = 3)
fc

fc |>
  filter(Country == "Sweden", .model=="drift_method") |> 
  autoplot(gdppc) +
  labs(title = "GDP per capita for Sweden", y = "$US")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Generates 3-year-ahead forecasts for all models and countries.
- Plots the drift method forecast for Sweden with historical data.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Examine the forecast values and intervals.
- Compare the naive vs drift forecast patterns.
:::

## E. Benchmark methods for holidays data

Now shifting to benchmark methods for the holidays series.

```r
holidays <- tourism |>
  filter(State %in% c("Victoria", "Queensland")) |>
  filter(Purpose == "Holiday") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(Trips = sum(Trips), .by = c("State", "Quarter")) |> 
  as_tsibble(index = Quarter, key = State)

holidays |> autoplot()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Creates the holidays tsibble as in previous weeks.
- Plots the series to visualize the data.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Review the seasonal and trend patterns in the holidays data.
- Compare Victoria and Queensland.
:::

## F. Fit benchmark models

Fit all four benchmark methods to the holidays data.

```r
fit_benchmarks <- holidays |>
  model(
    mean = MEAN(Trips),
    naive = NAIVE(Trips),
    drift = RW(Trips ~ drift()),
    snaive = SNAIVE(Trips)
  )
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Fits mean, naive, drift, and seasonal naive models.
- These are the standard benchmark methods.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Each model has different assumptions about the data.
- Consider which might be most appropriate for seasonal data.
:::

## G. Generate and plot forecasts

Produce 4-year-ahead forecasts and visualize them.

```r
fc_benchmarks <- fit_benchmarks |> forecast(h = 16)
fc_benchmarks |> autoplot(holidays)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Forecasts 16 quarters (4 years) ahead.
- Plots all benchmark forecasts with historical data.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Compare the forecast behaviors of different benchmarks.
- Look at how they handle seasonality and trends.
:::

## H. Check residuals

Plot residuals from the most appropriate benchmark.

```r
fit_benchmarks |>
  filter(State == "Victoria", .model == "snaive") |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Selects the seasonal naive model for Victoria.
- Plots residual diagnostics.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Check for patterns in residuals that indicate model inadequacy.
- Assess autocorrelation and distribution.
:::

## I. Test for white noise

Test if residuals are white noise.

```r
fit_benchmarks |>
  filter(State == "Victoria", .model == "snaive") |>
  augment() |>
  features(.resid, ljung_box, lag = 10)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Performs Ljung-Box test on residuals for autocorrelation.
- Tests the null hypothesis of white noise.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- If p-value < 0.05, reject white noise (autocorrelation present).
- Conclude on model adequacy.
:::

## J. Plot forecast intervals

Show point and interval forecasts.

```r
fc_benchmarks |>
  filter(State == "Victoria", .model == "snaive") |>
  autoplot(holidays) +
  labs(title = "Seasonal naive forecasts for Victoria")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Plots the forecast with prediction intervals.
- Focuses on seasonal naive for Victoria.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Examine the width of prediction intervals.
- Consider the uncertainty in the forecasts.
:::

## K. Try decomposition model

Fit a decomposition forecasting model.

```r
fit_decomp <- holidays |>
  model(stl = STL(Trips))

fc_decomp <- fit_decomp |> forecast(h = 16)
fc_decomp |> autoplot(holidays)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Fits an STL decomposition model.
- Generates forecasts based on the decomposition.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Compare decomposition forecasts to benchmarks.
- See how it handles trend and seasonality.
:::

## L. Evaluate accuracy

Use accuracy() to compare benchmark fits.

```r
accuracy(fit_benchmarks)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Calculates in-sample accuracy measures for all models.
- Compares RMSE and other metrics.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Identify which benchmark performs best.
- Consider the metrics and their implications.
:::

## M. Test set evaluation

Check forecast accuracy on last 3 years.

```r
holidays_train <- holidays |> filter(Quarter < yearquarter("2015 Q1"))
fit_train <- holidays_train |>
  model(
    mean = MEAN(Trips),
    naive = NAIVE(Trips),
    drift = RW(Trips ~ drift()),
    snaive = SNAIVE(Trips)
  )

fc_test <- fit_train |> forecast(h = 12)
accuracy(fc_test, holidays)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Fits models to training data (up to 2014).
- Forecasts the test period (2015-2017).
- Evaluates accuracy on held-out data.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- Compare test set performance to in-sample.
- See if rankings change.
:::

## N. Time series cross-validation

Use TSCV for robust evaluation.

```r
holidays |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 20, .step = 4) |>
  model(snaive = SNAIVE(Trips)) |>
  forecast(h = 4) |>
  accuracy(holidays)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this code is doing

- Performs time series cross-validation.
- Evaluates seasonal naive on rolling windows.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## What to notice

- TSCV provides more reliable accuracy estimates.
- Compare to previous evaluation methods.
:::
